thesis: All visual representation can be analysed along five independent axes, each a spectrum between two poles. These poles describe not better or worse but fundamentally different modes of seeing — different orientations of taste and interest in the world. The shift from one pole to its opposite is not progress or decay but a transformation in decorative feeling that runs deeper than subject matter or technique. The five axes are: linear vs. painterly, plane vs. recession, closed vs. open form, multiplicity vs. unity, and absolute clarity vs. relative clarity.

criteria.label: Linear vs. Painterly
criteria.definition: Linear style sees in lines — the sense and beauty of things is sought in the outline. The eye is led along boundaries and induced to feel along the edges. Form is apprehended as tangible, plastically felt, with every contour a confident track the spectator can entrust himself to. Painterly style sees in masses — attention withdraws from edges, and the primary impression is of patches of light, shadow, and colour. Forms are no longer bounded but participate in a ceaselessly emanating movement. The painterly eye perceives everything as vibrating and suffers nothing to settle into definite lines and surfaces.
diagnostic_questions: Are contours carrying the composition, or are tonal masses?
Can you trace a confident edge around each form, or do forms bleed into each other through light and shadow?
Does the image appeal to the tactile sense (you could feel along the edges) or purely to the visual sense (you see light and atmosphere)?
Do separate forms remain distinct, or do they coalesce in a general tonal movement?

pole_a: Sharp, evenly firm boundaries around forms
Silhouettes that coincide with the plastic form of the object
Modelling shadows that follow the form completely
Distinct separation of figure and ground
Each form can be isolated and still reads clearly
pole_b: Edges that are unstressed or indeterminate
Lights and shadows pursuing each other independently of form boundaries
Forms dissolving into a common tonal or chromatic movement
Figure and ground sharing a visual substance — 'as if everything were of the same stuff'
The total picture, not the separate form, is what counts

toward_a: Make modelling shadows follow the plastic form more closely
Separate figure from ground more decisively
Give each form a self-sufficient silhouette
toward_b: Soften or dissolve boundary edges
Let light and shadow move across forms independently of their contours
Create tonal connections between separate forms
Reduce the tactile clarity of individual shapes in favour of atmospheric unity

common_misreadings: Treating 'painterly' as a compliment and 'linear' as rigid — both are complete modes of seeing
Confusing 'painterly' with 'blurry' or 'soft focus' — the painterly has its own rigorous order of masses
Confusing 'linear' with 'outline drawing' — linear includes fully modelled form where edges still dominate
The painterly is not a higher stage in the imitation of nature, but a totally different solution

criteria.label: Plane vs. Recession
criteria.definition: Planar style organises the composition in layers parallel to the picture surface — forms are stratified in bands and the picture space reads as a sequence of discrete planes (front, middle, back). Colour lies in layers; spatial relations are presented as a stacking of strips. Recessional style draws the eye into continuous depth — diagonals, overlapping, exaggerated foregrounds, and atmospheric perspective enforce an immediate experience of recession rather than a series of discrete strata.
diagnostic_questions: Do the main forms line up in parallel planes, or do diagonals pull the eye inward?
Can the composition be described as a stack of horizontal strips?
Is depth experienced as discrete layers or as a continuous flow?
Are foreground and background linked by visual forces, or do they remain separate strata?

pole_a: Figures and forms arranged in a stage-like frieze parallel to the picture surface
Colour gradations proceeding in clear, quiet zones from front to back
Spatial depth achieved through stratification, not through continuous flow
No violent perspective diminution; sizes graduate gently across planes
pole_b: Diagonal movements drawing the eye from foreground into depth
Exaggerated foreground scale forcing a recessional reading
Light passing freely across depth without respecting planar strata
Overlapping and enframing used to drive things backward
Colour perspective creating continuous spatial flow rather than bands

toward_a: Align major forms parallel to the picture plane
Organise depth into clear, separate horizontal strata
Reduce diagonal movements that pull the eye inward
Let colour grade in distinct zones from front to back
toward_b: Introduce diagonal movements linking foreground and background
Exaggerate scale differences between near and far elements
Let light and colour flow continuously through depth rather than in bands
Use overlapping to enforce a recessional reading

common_misreadings: Confusing 'planar' with 'flat' — planar images have depth, but it is organised in discrete layers
Treating recession as automatically more sophisticated or skilful
Every picture has recession; the question is whether space organises itself into planes or is experienced as a homogeneous recessional movement

criteria.label: Closed Form vs. Open Form
criteria.definition: Closed form makes of the picture a self-contained entity, pointing everywhere back to itself. Verticals and horizontals dominate, the contents are disposed so that edge lines and corner angles re-echo in the composition, and the picture is built on stable equilibrium. Open form everywhere points beyond itself and purposely looks limitless. The diagonal undermines the rectangularity of the picture space; symmetry is replaced by oscillating balance; the picture looks like a piece cut from the visible world rather than a composition invented for its surface.
diagnostic_questions: Does the composition resolve within its borders, or does it suggest continuation beyond the frame?
Do major axes echo the frame edges (vertical/horizontal dominance) or cut across them (diagonal dominance)?
Is the equilibrium stable (closed) or oscillating/unstable (open)?
Does the picture look like it was composed for its surface, or like a passing show?

pole_a: Verticals and horizontals dominate as directions
Symmetry or clear bilateral balance
Edge lines and corner angles echoed in the composition
Pure aspects (full-face, profile) used deliberately
Every element looks intentional and placed for this surface
The form has the character of inevitability — nothing could be moved
pole_b: Diagonal as the main direction
Asymmetric distribution with unstable, oscillating balance
Content parting company with the frame — things cut off at edges
Avoidance of pure full-face and profile in favour of intermediate aspects
The picture looks accidental, a passing moment, not staged
Geometry concealed; the tectonic scaffolding hidden

toward_a: Let the composition echo the geometry of its frame
Stabilise the balance toward bilateral equilibrium
Show forms in their clearest, most characteristic aspects
toward_b: Introduce diagonal movement that cuts across the frame geometry
Shift balance from stable to oscillating
Let elements at the edges suggest a world continuing beyond the frame
Conceal the tectonic scaffolding so the composition looks less staged

common_misreadings: Confusing closed form with rigidity — closed compositions can be powerfully dynamic within their self-containment
Confusing open form with poor composition — open form has secret limits and is self-contained in the aesthetic sense
This is not only about edge behaviour but about the whole compositional logic: revealed law vs. concealed law

criteria.label: Multiplicity vs. Unity
criteria.definition: Multiplicity is an articulated system in which the parts, though harmoniously interdependent, maintain independent significance — each is a self-sufficient element that can be separately apprehended. Unity is a homogeneous flow in which the individual part has abdicated its independence to the whole; a dominating total motive governs, and forms cannot be extracted without loss. The sixteenth century is not discredited by the seventeenth, for this is not a qualitative difference but something totally new.
diagnostic_questions: Can individual elements be isolated and still 'work,' or does meaning collapse without the whole?
Is the image an 'articulated system with independent parts' or a 'unified stream'?
Is there a dominating total motive to which everything subordinates, or do parts co-ordinate as equals?
Has the separate detail abdicated its independence, or does it speak for itself?

pole_a: Each element is worked out with independent significance
Parts condition each other but maintain their own centre of gravity
Co-ordination of equivalent components
The beauty of the separate part — a column, a panel, a figure — at rest within itself
The whole is a team of soloists
pole_b: One dominant motive governs the entire composition
Individual forms cannot be detached without the whole losing coherence
Parts are fused in a mass effect — a unified stream
Light, colour, or compositional movement creates a single current
The whole is an orchestra — every part draws life only from the ensemble

toward_a: Give individual elements more independent presence and self-sufficiency
Let parts maintain their own proportional beauty rather than serving only the whole
Develop co-ordination among equals rather than subordination to a dominant motive
toward_b: Develop a dominating total motive that governs all elements
Fuse separate elements into a unified mass or stream
Let individual forms abdicate independence in favour of the overall effect
Create a single dominant movement of light, tone, or form that carries the composition

common_misreadings: Treating unity as always superior to multiplicity — 'the sixteenth century is not discredited by the seventeenth'
Confusing multiplicity with clutter — multiplicity is an articulated system, not disorder
Confusing unity with simplicity — a unified composition can be very complex

criteria.label: Absolute Clarity vs. Relative Clarity
criteria.definition: Absolute clarity presents every form in its most complete, exhaustive, and characteristic aspect — nothing is hidden, foreshortened past recognition, or left ambiguous. The form and its representation coincide; the image explains itself fully. Relative clarity withdraws from exhaustive presentation — forms are partially concealed, overlapping, in shadow, or shown in aspects that do not fully disclose them. The image withholds and relies on the viewer to complete what is suggested.
diagnostic_questions: Is every element shown in its most legible, characteristic aspect?
Are forms partially hidden, overlapping, in shadow, or foreshortened?
Does the image explain itself fully or ask the viewer to complete it?
Does the lighting serve the distinctness of objects, or does it pass over them?

pole_a: Forms shown in their most characteristic aspects (frontal, profile)
Lighting subserves the distinctness of objects
Nothing essential is hidden or cut off
The form and its picture coincide — tactile and visual agree
Each element invites exhaustive scrutiny
pole_b: Forms partially concealed by overlapping, shadow, or oblique aspect
Lighting passes over forms, partially veiling them
A sense of 'a secret remains to be guessed'
The picture gives only as much as a general view yields — not pursuing every detail
Unified visual perception from one distance rather than separate scrutiny of each part

toward_a: Show each form in its most legible, characteristic aspect
Let lighting fully reveal the structure of objects
Remove obscuring overlaps or shadows that hide essential features
toward_b: Partially veil forms through overlapping, shadow, or oblique angles
Let lighting move across forms independently of their structure
Create areas that suggest rather than fully disclose
Design for a general impression at one viewing distance rather than part-by-part scrutiny

common_misreadings: Wölfflin uses 'unclearness' (Unklarheit) non-pejoratively — it is a deliberate aesthetic strategy, not a flaw
Absolute clarity does not mean photographic detail — it means showing the form in its most exhaustive aspect
Relative clarity is not poor execution — it is the active withholding of full disclosure for aesthetic effect

anti_goals: Must not rank one pole above the other — 'the linear style developed values which the painterly style no longer possessed and no longer wanted to possess'
Must not reduce the analysis to a period classification ('is this Renaissance or Baroque?') — the categories describe visual properties, not historical labels
Must not treat the five axes as a checklist of features to have or lack — they are spectra to locate a position on
Must not conflate the axes — they are independent. An image can be linear but recessional, closed but unified
Must not give generic composition advice unrelated to the five polarities
Must not confuse these categories with other frameworks (Gestalt grouping, colour theory, design principles)
Must not treat the painterly as 'more advanced' or 'more realistic' — it is 'not a higher stage in the solution of the one problem of the imitation of nature, but a totally different solution'

tensions.label: Description vs. prescription
tensions.description: Wölfflin's categories are descriptive — they map where an image falls, not where it should fall. A critic must locate, not prescribe. But in a generative feedback loop, some directional guidance is needed. The tension: use the axes to diagnose and suggest movement along a spectrum, not to grade.

tensions.label: Independence of axes vs. coherence
tensions.description: The five axes are theoretically independent, yet historically they tend to correlate (linear + planar + closed + multiple + clear = 'classic'; their opposites = 'baroque'). An image that mixes poles across axes may be intentionally hybrid or may be incoherent. The critic must note the mixture without automatically treating it as a defect.

tensions.label: Visual properties vs. subject matter
tensions.description: Wölfflin insists the categories describe visual organisation, not content. But some subject matter naturally invites one pole (a crowd scene is 'picturesque'). The critic must separate the visual analysis from the thematic affordance.

tensions.label: Period-bound origins vs. general applicability
tensions.description: Wölfflin derived his categories from Renaissance→Baroque comparison, but he claims they describe universal visual possibilities. Applying them to non-Western or contemporary art requires care — the axes are reusable, but the historical narrative is not.

citations.claim: Linear sees in lines, painterly sees in masses
citations.quote_or_paraphrase: Linear vision means that the sense and beauty of things is first sought in the outline — interior forms have their outline too — that the eye is led along the boundaries and induced to feel along the edges, while seeing in masses takes place where the attention withdraws from the edges.

citations.claim: The painterly is not a higher stage but a different solution
citations.quote_or_paraphrase: The painterly is not a higher stage in the solution of the one problem of the imitation of nature, but a totally different solution. Only where decorative feeling has changed can we expect a transformation of the mode of representation.

The linear style developed values which the painterly style no longer possessed and no longer wanted to possess. They are two conceptions of the world, differently orientated in taste and in their interest in the world, and yet each capable of giving a perfect picture of visible things.

Linear style is the style of distinctness plastically felt. The evenly firm and clear boundaries of solid objects give the spectator a feeling of security, as if he could move along them with his fingers. The tactile picture has become the visual picture — the most decisive revolution which art history knows.

citations.claim: Plane composition as stratification in bands
citations.quote_or_paraphrase: Every picture has recession, but the recession has a very different effect according to whether the space organises itself into planes or is experienced as a homogeneous recessional movement.

A style of composition which, with more or less tectonic means, makes of the picture a self-contained entity, pointing everywhere back to itself, while the style of open form everywhere points out beyond itself and purposely looks limitless.

citations.claim: Multiplicity as articulated independence of parts
citations.quote_or_paraphrase: There stand opposed the multiple unity of the sixteenth century and the unified unity of the seventeenth: in other words, the articulated system of forms of classic art and the (endless) flow of the baroque.
There is no such thing as objective vision, and form and colour are always apprehended differently according to temperament.

confidence_notes: The 'clearness/unclearness' axis is the most difficult to operationalize for generated images, since it partly depends on intentional concealment and suggestion, which are hard to quantify.
Wölfflin's examples are all representational painting, sculpture, and architecture. Applying his categories to fully abstract or non-Western images requires extrapolation beyond his explicit scope.

The correlation between axes (linear tends to go with planar, closed, multiple, and clear) is historically observed but not theoretically necessary. The critic should note but not enforce this correlation.
